answer.rationale: Memory c2 is the load-bearing claim: it says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply, onboarded quickly, and invoiced accurately. If that record holds, switching primary supply is the only option that plausibly meets the 18% cut mandate without a second negotiation the incumbent has already refused. Memory c6 (multi-year volume pricing with the incumbent) is blocked this cycle by the incumbent's refusal to reopen price. Memory c4 (renegotiate at renewal) likewise assumes willingness to move on price, which has been withdrawn. Adding a second source (c3) protects against single-point failure but does not by itself deliver the required cost reduction. Deferring (c5) is viable only for non-critical spend; here the primary contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so deferral risks the assembly line, which is already at 94% committed volume with no buffer. I verify c2 because the switch decision stands or falls on whether that prior low-cost vendor transition was genuinely clean and fast. If the archived record confirms it, I commit to switching primary supply to that vendor within the 14-day window, using the incumbent refusal as leverage in a brief counter before signature. If the record shows any delivery or quality issues not captured in the summary, I fall back to renew_incumbent at current terms plus an immediate parallel RFP, accepting that the 18% target slips to next review.
